concept.overview: Terraform is an Infrastructure as Code (IaC) tool that lets you define cloud and on-prem infrastructure — servers, networks, databases, DNS — in declarative configuration files. You describe the desired end state in HCL (HashiCorp Configuration Language), and Terraform figures out the create/update/delete actions needed to reach it, then applies them through provider APIs. Because the configuration is version-controlled code, infrastructure becomes reproducible, reviewable, and automatable, the same way application code is.
concept.whyItMatters: Manually clicking through cloud consoles is slow, error-prone, and impossible to audit or reproduce. Terraform makes infrastructure declarative and idempotent: the same config yields the same environment every time, whether it's the first apply or the hundredth. It enables safe change previews (plan), team collaboration through shared state, and multi-cloud provisioning from one workflow — the foundation of modern platform engineering.
useCases: Provisioning entire environments (VPC, subnets, EC2, RDS) reproducibly
Spinning up identical dev/staging/prod stacks from the same modules
Managing DNS, IAM, and Kubernetes clusters as versioned code
Previewing and reviewing infrastructure changes before they happen
Tearing down ephemeral environments to control cost
concept.architecture: You write .tf files declaring providers (AWS, GCP, etc.) and resources. 'terraform init' downloads provider plugins and configures the backend. Terraform maintains a state file that maps your configuration to real-world resource IDs. 'terraform plan' diffs desired config against state and shows the exact changes; 'terraform apply' executes them via provider APIs and updates state. State should live in a remote backend (e.g., S3 with DynamoDB locking) so teams share one source of truth and avoid concurrent corruption. Reusable groups of resources are packaged as modules; variables and outputs parameterize and expose values.

definitions.def: A plugin that lets Terraform manage a specific platform's resources (AWS, Azure, etc.).
A single infrastructure object declared in HCL, e.g., aws_instance.
Terraform's record mapping config to real resource IDs; the source of truth for diffs.
A preview of the actions Terraform will take to reach the desired state.
A reusable, parameterized bundle of resources.
Inputs that parameterize config and values exposed after apply.

commands.desc: Initialize the working directory, download providers, configure backend.
Preview changes and save the plan to a file.
Apply exactly the reviewed, saved plan.
Bring an existing resource under Terraform management.
Create an isolated state workspace for an environment.
Scope a plan to a specific resource (use sparingly).
Force a resource to be recreated on next apply.

bestPractices: Store state remotely (e.g., S3) with locking (DynamoDB) so teams don't corrupt it.
Always run and review 'terraform plan' before apply; commit plans in CI.
Never edit resources by hand in the console — it causes state drift.
Use modules and variables to keep environments DRY and consistent.
Keep secrets out of state where possible and never commit .tfstate to Git.
pitfalls: Committing terraform.tfstate to Git — it can contain secrets and causes conflicts.
Manual console changes that drift from state, breaking the next apply.
Running apply without reading the plan and destroying production resources.
No state locking, letting two applies corrupt shared state.
Hardcoding values instead of using variables, blocking reuse across environments.
cheatSheet: Safe workflow: init -> fmt -> validate -> plan -> apply
Remote state (S3): backend "s3" { bucket, key, region, dynamodb_table }
Loop with count: count = 3 ; each = count.index
Loop with for_each over a set/map for named resources

quiz.question: What does 'terraform plan' do?
options: Previews the actions needed to reach desired state
quiz.explanation: plan diffs config against state and shows what would change, without applying.

quiz.question: The Terraform state file maps your configuration to real resource IDs.
quiz.explanation: State is how Terraform tracks which real resources correspond to your config.

quiz.question: Why store state in a remote backend like S3 with locking?
options: So teams share one state and avoid concurrent corruption
quiz.explanation: Remote state with locking gives a shared source of truth and prevents simultaneous corrupting applies.

quiz.question: You should commit terraform.tfstate to your Git repository.
quiz.explanation: State can contain secrets and causes conflicts; keep it in a remote backend, not Git.

quiz.question: What is state drift?
options: Real infrastructure changed outside Terraform, diverging from state
quiz.explanation: Drift happens when resources are changed manually, so state no longer matches reality.

quiz.question: What does a Terraform module provide?
options: A reusable, parameterized group of resources
quiz.explanation: Modules package resources for reuse across environments and projects.

quiz.question: A teammate manually resized an instance in the console. Next 'terraform apply' will:
options: Detect drift and try to revert it to the config's value
quiz.explanation: Terraform reconciles to desired state, so it plans to change the resource back unless config is updated.

quiz.question: Which command safely applies exactly what you reviewed?
options: terraform plan -out=tfplan then terraform apply tfplan
quiz.explanation: Saving the plan and applying that file guarantees you apply exactly the reviewed changes.

quiz.question: Terraform is declarative and idempotent — re-running apply on unchanged config makes no changes.
quiz.explanation: If reality matches desired state, apply is a no-op.

quiz.question: How do you bring an existing, manually created resource under Terraform?
quiz.explanation: terraform import maps an existing resource ID into state.

quiz.question: You must provision identical staging and prod stacks. Best approach?
options: Use modules with variables and separate state/workspaces
quiz.explanation: Modules plus variables and per-environment state keep stacks DRY and consistent.

quiz.question: What does 'terraform init' primarily do?
options: Downloads providers and configures the backend
quiz.explanation: init prepares the working directory: providers, modules, and backend.

quiz.question: Two engineers run 'terraform apply' at the same time on shared local state. Risk?
options: State corruption from concurrent writes; use remote state with locking
quiz.explanation: Concurrent applies on unlocked shared state can corrupt it; remote locking prevents this.

tasks.title: Provision a single resource
steps: Write a provider block and one resource (e.g., a local_file or a cloud resource in a sandbox)
Run terraform plan and read the output
Run terraform apply and then terraform destroy
successCriteria: plan shows the resource to be created
apply creates it and destroy removes it

tasks.title: Parameterize with variables and outputs
steps: Extract hardcoded values into variables with defaults
Add an outputs.tf exposing a useful attribute
Override a variable via -var or a tfvars file
successCriteria: Changing a variable changes the plan
terraform output prints the exposed value

tasks.title: Refactor into a module with remote state
steps: Move resources into a reusable module directory
Configure an S3 (or equivalent) remote backend with locking
Call the module for two workspaces/environments
Verify state is stored remotely and locked during apply
successCriteria: The same module provisions two environments
State lives in the remote backend, not locally

tasks.title: Build a small VPC stack
steps: Declare a VPC, public and private subnets, and a route table
Add an EC2 instance in the public subnet with a security group
Plan, review, and apply the stack
Destroy it to control cost when done
successCriteria: The network and instance are created as planned
A clean destroy removes all managed resources
